content: In many resource-limited countries, while it is desirable to develop policies for access to third-line antiretroviral therapy (ART), this should not compromise access to firstand second-line ART. For individuals whose first-line non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based regimen and second-line dolutegravir (DTG)-based ART have failed, protease inhibitor (PI)-based ART may be considered as a third-line option. The choice of PI (e.g., atazanavir/ritonavir [ATV/r], darunavir/ritonavir [DRV/r], or lopinavir/ritonavir [LPV/r]) should be guided by factors such as cost, availability, and convenience. Where feasible, genotyping can be performed to optimize third-line regimen selection, including the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) backbone. There is limited research on the use of newer antiretroviral (ARV) drugs as part of third-line regimens for children, adolescents, and pregnant or breastfeeding women. Pharmacokinetic and safety data for these populations are particularly lacking. Consequently, strategies must balance the benefits and risks when second-line ART fails. Based on available data, DRV and DTG are recommended for third-line regimens in children, though there is uncertainty about whether these drugs should be used in combination or as part of a standard NRTI-based regimen. DRV cannot be used in children under three years of age and is only available in select countries through donation programs. Raltegravir (RAL) is an alternative for children who fail PI-based second-line ART and should be considered when DTG cannot be used. For children with no new ARV options after second-line failure, continuing a tolerated regimen is recommended, similar to adults. If ART is discontinued, attention should be given to preventing opportunistic infections, relieving symptoms, and managing pain. There is also limited data on the use of newer third-line drugs in pregnant or breastfeeding women. Further research is needed to guide third-line ART strategies in resource-limited settings. Priorities include monitoring critical outcomes for individuals on second-line ART, developing heat-stable formulations of DRV/r, and evaluating the pharmacokinetics, safety, and efficacy of new drugs in children, adolescents, and pregnant women. Viral load testing is the preferred method for monitoring ART and diagnosing treatment failure. Routine viral load monitoring should be conducted at six months, 12 months, and annually thereafter for individuals established on ART. Point-of-care viral load testing may be used where available. In settings where viral load testing is not routinely available, CD4 cell count and clinical monitoring should be used to diagnose treatment failure. Dried blood spot specimens can be used to determine HIV viral load, with a threshold of 1,000 copies/mL to define virological failure. Plasma specimens are preferred, but dried blood spots are recommended in settings with logistical or operational barriers to plasma testing. Clinical and diagnostic assessments are essential after an HIV diagnosis to evaluate for toxicity, coinfections, noncommunicable diseases, and other comorbidities that may affect treatment response. Recommended tests include viral load testing, CD4 cell count, serum creatinine, and estimated glomerular filtration rate for tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) users, as well as pregnancy tests for women of childbearing potential on DTG or efavirenz (EFV). Hepatitis B serology should be performed at baseline to identify HIV/HBV coinfection, and TDF-containing ART should be initiated in such cases. Monitoring for noncommunicable diseases, such as hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and tuberculosis, is also recommended. Viral load testing provides an early and accurate indication of treatment failure, allowing timely switching from first-line to second-line drugs and reducing the accumulation of drug resistance mutations. It also helps differentiate between treatment failure and non-adherence. Adherence counseling should be provided at all visits to ensure viral suppression is maintained. For individuals with viral loads between 50 and 1,000 copies/mL, enhanced adherence counseling and repeat viral load testing after three months are recommended. Switching ART should be considered after a second elevated viral load result. For children, viral suppression may take longer than in adults. For example, data from the ARROW trial showed that only 40% and 57% of children on LPV/r-based regimens achieved viral suppression to <400 copies/mL at one and three months, respectively, compared to 94% by six months. This highlights the need for tailored approaches to monitoring and managing ART in pediatric populations.
